Series::sin¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::sin() const -> Series
Series& Series::sin_()

What It Does¶

Applies the sine transform elementwise.

Each input element is interpreted as an angle in radians. The output is the sine of that angle, so every finite real input maps into [-1, 1].

This is a pure value transform:

  • shape is preserved

  • each element is independent

  • no broadcasting enters the picture

Because sine is periodic, sin() is useful when the cyclic nature of the input matters more than its raw magnitude.

Parameters¶

None.

This is a zero-argument transform on self.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, where each element has been replaced by its sine.

Gradient¶

sin(x) is differentiable for all real inputs, with derivative cos(x).

That means:

  • the backward multiplier is 1 at zero

  • it drops to 0 at odd multiples of pi / 2

  • it becomes negative where cosine is negative

The verified reverse-mode example below reflects that behavior on the current surface.

In-Place Form¶

sin_() is the in-place sibling of sin(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0});

auto& ref = x.sin_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0.84147098]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. Standard anchor angles show the basic sine cycle.

const double pi = 3.14159265358979323846;
pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-pi / 2.0, 0.0, pi / 2.0, pi}).sin());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0000e+00, 0.0000e+00, 1.0000e+00, 1.2246e-16]

Example 2. Matrices keep their layout while values transform elementwise.

const double pi = 3.14159265358979323846;
std::cout << pluss::make_series({
    {0.0, pi / 2.0},
    {pi, 3.0 * pi / 2.0},
}).sin();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 1],
  [1.2246468e-16, -1]]

Example 3. Reverse-mode sensitivity follows cos(x).

const double pi = 3.14159265358979323846;
auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, pi / 2.0, pi});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto out = x.sin();
out.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << out << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 1.2246468e-16]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 6.123234e-17, -1]

Example 4. Non-contiguous views can still be transformed normally.

const double pi = 3.14159265358979323846;
auto view = pluss::make_series({
    {0.0, pi / 6.0, pi / 3.0},
    {pi / 2.0, 2.0 * pi / 3.0, 5.0 * pi / 6.0},
}).transpose(0, 1);

std::cout << view.sin();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 1],
  [0.5, 0.8660254],
  [0.8660254, 0.5]]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Inputs are interpreted in radians.

  • Exact mathematical zeros at angles such as pi can show up as tiny floating residues like 1.2246e-16.

  • Periodicity can collapse distinct raw values into the same transformed value.

Summary¶

Use sin() for radian-valued periodic transforms when phase matters. Expect shape preservation, bounded outputs, and normal floating approximations at special angles.

See Also¶

  • Series::cos: phase-shifted companion.

  • Series::tan: tangent ratio transform.

  • Series::asin: inverse sine on [-1, 1].
